The source records that it was used to mark the night watches, to call the soldiers with the classicum and to pass on orders. Only Respighi is recorded as writing for a range, using six buccinae of different pitch; the source does not say how the volume was controlled. Against horns of the same family it is like the cornu but has a supporting crossbar, which the player grips to steady it; in later works the 'buccine' may be replaced by modern saxhorns, flugelhorns or trumpets.

布奇那號的聆聽場合首先見於古代羅馬軍樂，用於宣告夜間崗哨、以特殊信號召集士兵與傳: The buccina is first heard in ancient Roman military music, used to announce the night watch, to call soldiers with a special signal and to pass on orders. In later music it appears in orchestral and ceremonial works: the last movement of Respighi's Pini di Roma calls for six instruments labelled Buccine and expects them to be played on modern saxhorns or flugelhorns; the opening of Feste romane also calls for three, which may be replaced by trumpets. During the French Revolution, the music that François Joseph Gossec wrote for the transfer of Voltaire's remains to the Panthéon also used revived buccinae and tubae curvae.
布奇那號起源於古代羅馬軍隊，是與cornu相似的軍號，用於夜間崗哨、召喚士兵與傳: The buccina comes from the army of ancient Rome; it is a military horn like the cornu, used for the night watch, for calling soldiers and for passing on orders. It is regarded as an ancestor of the trumpet and the trombone, and the German word Posaune comes from its name. During the French Revolution the buccina was revived along with the tuba curva, and was first used on 11 July 1791 in Gossec's music for the transfer of Voltaire's body to the Panthéon. Respighi's orchestral works still label instruments Buccine, but modern saxhorns, flugelhorns or trumpets are expected instead.
